title: PART I

nodes.title: ITEM 1. BUSINESS
nodes.summary: ExxonMobil’s history, global operations, businesses, brands, research, and lower-emission opportunities are outlined, including its May 2024 Pioneer acquisition. The text describes industry competition, where to find segment and reserve data, its patent portfolio and technology licensing, and its long-term talent strategy, workforce diversity, and employee counts. It notes regulatory and environmental risks and points readers to related disclosures on materials, seasonality, government contracts, and foreign operations. It also explains online access to company filings and governance documents and SEC resources.

nodes.title: ITEM 1A. RISK FACTORS
Supply and Demand
nodes.summary: ExxonMobil identifies risks from commodity price and margin volatility, which can affect different business segments and proved reserves, and from uncertain markets, policy support, and technology for lower-emission and new businesses. Results may also be affected by economic downturns, geopolitical and trade disruptions, financial-market or currency instability, and pandemics; demand shifts from efficiency, weather, alternatives, technology, consumer preferences, and income; supply changes from production, capacity, quotas, regulation, funding, conflict, disasters, competitor disruptions, logistics, and technology; and interest rates, inflation, exchange rates, dollar usage, local market conditions, and losses on hedging or trading instruments.

nodes.title: Government and Political Factors
nodes.summary: ExxonMobil faces political and regulatory risks that may harm its operations and results: restricted access to resources, investment, trade, or markets; sanctions and business prohibitions that disadvantage it versus competitors; and weak or unstable legal systems that create unpredictable government actions, compliance difficulties, and contract-enforcement challenges. Laws, policies, and litigation may change taxes, royalties, prices, environmental and emissions rules, permits, incentives, technology standards, disclosures, or business requirements, and governments may cancel contracts, default, alter currencies, or expropriate assets. Remedies may be inadequate, and litigation, enforcement, punitive damages, and policy-driven lawsuits can be costly. Civil unrest, sabotage, piracy, terrorism, cyberattacks, security policies, strikes, or protests may raise costs or disrupt and halt operations.

nodes.title: Climate Change and the Energy Transition
nodes.summary: The text outlines uncertainties and risks in the energy transition: net-zero goals rely on hypothetical scenarios, evolving technologies, supportive policy, and timely investment decisions. Climate measures—including emissions rules, taxes, trade restrictions, mandates, and efforts to limit oil-and-gas financing or infrastructure—could raise costs, delay projects, weaken returns and hydrocarbon demand, and increase compliance burdens. ExxonMobil’s Low Carbon Solutions efforts include CCS, hydrogen, lower-emission fuels, lithium, efficiency, and research partnerships; success depends on developing cost-competitive technologies and infrastructure. Commercial growth also requires durable government and market support. Restricting hydrocarbons without matching demand reductions could cause price volatility, inflation, shortages, weaker growth, and policy shifts.

nodes.title: Operational and Other Factors
nodes.summary: The text outlines operational risks affecting ExxonMobil’s results: exploration and development success; complex project, portfolio, acquisition and divestment management, including costs, partners, contracts, liabilities and execution; operational efficiency and integration of Pioneer; technological innovation and R&D; safety, controls, environmental and enterprise-risk management; cybersecurity threats and third-party exposure; disaster preparedness; limited insurance; competition from private and state-owned firms, alternative energy and new entrants; and reputational risks. It notes forward-looking projections may differ materially and reports no unresolved staff comments. Item 1C describes cybersecurity governance, leadership, monitoring, layered controls, incident response, training, testing, information sharing and third-party risk practices; no known cyber risks have materially affected or are likely to materially affect the Corporation, though protection is not absolute.

ExxonMobil’s risks include volatile commodity prices, margins, demand, supply, currencies, and financial markets; economic, geopolitical, trade, pandemic, and market disruptions; and political, legal, regulatory, tax, sanctions, contract, security, and litigation challenges. Climate and energy-transition policies, uncertain technologies, investment, infrastructure, and market support may affect costs, projects, demand, and returns. Operational risks span exploration, projects, acquisitions, integration, technology, safety, environmental and enterprise controls, cybersecurity, disasters, insurance, competition, and reputation. The section notes forward-looking statements may differ materially and reports no unresolved staff comments; cybersecurity governance and controls are described, with no known materially affecting cyber risks, though protection is not absolute.

nodes.title: Reputation, Forward-Looking Statements, and Cybersecurity
nodes.summary: The page describes threats to ExxonMobil’s reputation and their possible effects on competition, approvals, financing, talent, and product demand, and notes that industry-wide events can also cause harm. It cautions that projections and plans are forward-looking and may differ materially from actual results. Item 1B reports no unresolved staff comments. Item 1C outlines cybersecurity oversight, management, controls, training, incident response, independent testing, information sharing, and risk-based third-party screening; no material cyber risks have been identified, though protection cannot be guaranteed.

Annual planning uses the Global Outlook and assumptions for prices, margins, volumes, costs, emissions pricing, and exchange rates. Investments are selected for competitiveness, assessed across market conditions, and reappraised to apply lessons to future projects.

nodes.title: BUSINESS ENVIRONMENT
Long-Term Business Outlook
Developing countries projected to drive energy demand growth
nodes.summary: ExxonMobil’s 2024 Outlook guides long-term planning using global energy fundamentals, multiple scenarios—including IPCC and IEA pathways—and indicators of changing policies, markets, and technology, while acknowledging substantial uncertainty. It projects population and economic growth to lift global energy demand nearly 15% by 2050, driven by developing countries, while developed-country use falls; efficiency lowers energy and emissions per output. Electricity demand rises over 75%, led by developing nations, with coal’s share declining and renewables, gas, and nuclear expanding. Transportation energy rises about 25%; efficiency and electric cars reduce light-duty fuel use, while commercial fleets largely retain liquid fuels. Industrial and residential/commercial demand grows, with cleaner energy gaining ground but oil remaining important as industrial feedstock. Liquid-fuel demand reaches about 110 million oil-equivalent barrels daily, supplied by conventional and diverse sources; natural-gas demand rises over 20%, especially in Asia Pacific, with conventional gas dominant, unconventional supply growing, and LNG trade expanding.

nodes.title: Oil and natural gas projected to play a critical role in the global energy mix
nodes.summary: ExxonMobil’s 2024 outlook projects a diverse global energy mix through 2050: oil remains the largest source at nearly 30%, natural gas rises above 25%, coal declines to about half natural gas’s share, nuclear grows, and renewables exceed 20%. Wind and solar grow more than 400% from 2023 to nearly 12% of the mix; other renewables exceed 10%. Decarbonizing industry requires stable policy and lower-carbon technologies: lower-emission fuels and electrification for transport, especially aviation; hydrogen and ammonia for industrial heat and commercial transport; and carbon capture and storage for power and hard-to-abate industries.

nodes.title: Significant oil and natural gas investment needed to meet projected global demand
nodes.summary: The discussion presents projected oil and natural gas supply and demand using IEA, ExxonMobil, and IPCC scenarios. ExxonMobil expects oil demand to exceed 100 million barrels per day through 2050; even average IPCC scenarios retain 66 million barrels per day. Oil output declines about 15% annually without investment, or 4% if limited to existing fields, still insufficient for projected demand. Meeting demand requires significant investment, technology, and growth in resources from discoveries and existing fields, even under decarbonization scenarios. Climate-policy timing and effects remain uncertain; the Outlook incorporates increasingly stringent policies and proxy CO₂ costs reaching $150 per metric ton in OECD and $100 in non-OECD nations by 2050. ExxonMobil monitors Paris Agreement commitments and other policies, while recognizing affordability and reliability needs; projections draw on internal analyses and public sources.

ExxonMobil’s 2024 Outlook uses global energy fundamentals, multiple scenarios, and policy, market, and technology indicators to inform long-term planning amid uncertainty. It projects rising demand through 2050, driven by developing economies, with efficiency moderating energy use and emissions. Oil and gas remain central alongside growing renewables, nuclear, and electricity; transport, industry, and buildings increasingly adopt cleaner energy and technologies such as hydrogen, electrification, and carbon capture. Meeting projected oil and gas demand requires substantial investment despite decarbonization pathways, with policy assumptions, affordability, reliability, and supply uncertainties considered.

nodes.title: Progress Reducing Emissions
nodes.summary: ExxonMobil aims to build competitive, cash-generative businesses while retaining investment flexibility across energy-transition scenarios. With technological progress and supportive policy, it targets net-zero Scope 1 and 2 emissions from operated assets by 2050, guided by asset-level roadmaps; heritage Permian assets target net zero by 2030 and Pioneer assets by 2035. By 2030 versus 2016, plans target reductions of 20–30% in corporate greenhouse-gas intensity, 70–80% in methane intensity, 40–50% in upstream greenhouse-gas intensity, and 60–70% in flaring intensity. Plans cover operated assets, including Pioneer and Denbury. The company is pursuing operational and customer emissions-reduction investments through Low Carbon Solutions, including carbon capture and storage, hydrogen, lower-emission fuels, Proxxima systems, carbon materials, and lithium. Denbury added over 900 miles of CO₂ pipelines and storage sites, creating the world’s largest CO₂ network and opportunities to serve Gulf Coast industry. Stable policy, technology advances, and market mechanisms are key to deploying lower-emission solutions.

nodes.title: Business Environment, Cost Savings, and Kazakhstan Transportation Risk
nodes.summary: In 2024, oil prices remained within their pre-COVID range; natural gas prices fell for most of the year before rising in the fourth quarter. Refining margins declined and chemical margins improved slightly but remained weak. Inflation eased unevenly, prompting U.S. and Eurozone rate cuts, while China faced deflation. The Corporation reported $12.1 billion in structural savings versus 2019, including $2.4 billion in 2024, and targets another $6 billion by 2030. title: BUSINESS RESULTS

nodes.title: Upstream
Key Recent Events
nodes.summary: ExxonMobil’s Upstream strategy prioritizes low-cost, advantaged projects, technology, and efficient project delivery while managing political and technical risks. Production is expected to grow and shift toward the Americas and unconventional, deepwater, and LNG resources, though volumes depend on project timing, operations, markets, policy, investment, and other factors; 2024 prices were within the pre-COVID decade’s range. Recent developments include strong Guyana FPSO output and plans for eight vessels by 2030; the Pioneer acquisition, Permian production growth and emissions targets; and progress on LNG projects in Papua New Guinea, Mozambique, and the United States. In 2024, earnings rose from advantaged-volume growth, structural savings, other items, improved derivative timing, and identified-item gains, but fell due to lower prices, divestments, and higher expenses. In 2023, earnings were reduced by lower prices, base-volume declines, higher expenses, unfavorable derivative timing, and identified-item losses, partly offset by advantaged growth, savings, and other gains. Identified-item explanations include asset impairments, divestments, Russia expropriation, and European taxes. Production tables cover regional crude oil, liquids, bitumen and synthetic oil, natural gas, and worldwide oil-equivalent output; gas conversion uses six million cubic feet per thousand barrels.

It explains the six-million-cubic-feet-per-thousand-barrels conversion and defines reconciliation drivers: net-interest and temporary price/spending entitlements, government mandates, divestments, and growth/other factors such as projects, acquisitions, downtime, demand, decline, and fiscal or commercial terms.

Reconciles year-over-year production changes, including growth, divestments, entitlements, mandates, projects, acquisitions, operational and market factors, and explains the gas-to-oil conversion.

nodes.title: Energy Products
nodes.summary: ExxonMobil Energy Products spans refining, logistics, trading, marketing, fuels, aromatics, catalysts and licensing. Earnings depend on volatile global refining margins and also operational performance, product mix and cost control; margins fell in 2024 amid supply growth and are expected to remain volatile. The text details renewable diesel and hydrofiner projects and refinery divestments/sale, 2022–2024 financial results and identified items, 2023 and 2024 earnings drivers, and 2022–2024 refinery throughput and energy-product sales by region and product.

nodes.title: Chemical Products
nodes.summary: ExxonMobil’s Chemical Products segment makes olefins, polyolefins and intermediates, using scale, integration and proprietary technology to supply affordable, more sustainable products. Long-term demand is expected to outpace economic growth. In 2024, industry margins remained below pre-COVID norms amid excess capacity; production was optimized, while reliability, high-value sales and low-cost North American ethane supported results. Key developments include a foreign-owned petrochemical complex in China planned for over 2.5 million metric tons of annual polyethylene and polypropylene capacity, and Baytown advanced-recycling expansion toward 1 billion pounds of global capacity by 2027. The text reports 2022–2024 U.S., non-U.S. and total earnings, identified items and adjusted earnings; explains 2024 and 2023 earnings drivers, including margins, volumes, cost savings, expenses and other items; and provides regional and worldwide chemical sales volumes.

In 2023, cash use was $34.3 billion, dividends totaled $14.9 billion, and 162 million shares worth $17.5 billion were repurchased. Contractual obligations include leases, debt, retirement and benefit liabilities, and purchase and capital commitments; certain commodity purchases are offset by related sales. Take-or-pay and unconditional obligations totaled $49.9 billion at year-end 2024, with $5.5 billion and $6.3 billion due in 2025 and 2026. title: CRITICAL ACCOUNTING ESTIMATES

nodes.title: Oil and Natural Gas Reserves
nodes.summary: The Corporation’s financial reporting reflects its integrated oil, gas, petrochemical, specialty-products, and lower-emission businesses. GAAP statements require management estimates and judgments; accounting policies are in Note 1. Proved-reserve estimates follow a disciplined, technically reviewed approval process without quantitative reserve targets tied to compensation. SEC-defined proved reserves are economically recoverable under current conditions and prices based on annual first-of-month averages; they comprise developed and undeveloped reserves, with undeveloped reserves generally requiring an adopted plan for drilling within five years. Recovery timing and volumes face operational, regulatory, policy, market, and price uncertainties. Unproved reserves include probable reserves, which are at least as likely as not to be recovered with proved reserves. Reserve estimates may be revised as data, prices, costs, development strategies, or facility capacity change.

nodes.title: Depreciation and Business Combination Valuation
key_items: Fair Value Used in Business Combinations

Straight-line or adjusted reserve-based methods apply when needed for an equitable allocation over an asset’s useful life. Business-combination purchase prices are allocated to assets and liabilities at estimated acquisition-date fair values, with any excess recorded as goodwill. For ExxonMobil’s May 2024 Pioneer acquisition, significant property valuations used discounted cash flow models and assumptions about production, prices, costs, and risk-adjusted discount rates; these judgments may differ from actual results. See Note 21 for details.

title: Note 14. Long-Term Debt
summary: The note reports 2024 long-term debt of $36.755 billion, including U.S.- and foreign-currency debt, excluding $4.892 billion due within one year; maturities for 2026–2029, $1.3 billion in unused credit lines, and a perfectly effective $3.1 billion Euro-denominated net-investment hedge are disclosed. A 2024/2023 debt table lists corporate, Euro, subsidiary, acquired-company, industrial-bond, and lease obligations by rate and maturity, average rates, total debt, and related premiums, discounts, hedge-accounting effects, and issuance costs.

title: Note 15. Incentive Program
summary: The 2003 Incentive Program permits stock options, SARs, restricted stock, and other awards for eligible employees; sets pricing, 10-year maximum option/SAR terms, a 220-million-share cap, forfeiture rules, and no fixed end date. At year-end 2024, 47 million shares remained. The note details restricted-award grants, service-period expense recognition, stock or cash settlement, transfer restrictions and forfeiture, vesting schedules, and conversion of Pioneer LTIP awards following the May 2024 acquisition, including its three-year vesting and remaining share capacity. It presents 2024 award activity and grant-date values, grant prices and values for 2022–2024, and compensation costs, tax benefits, unrecognized costs and recognition period, vested-award fair values, and cash settlement payments.

title: Note 16. Litigation and Other Contingencies
summary: Note 16 describes litigation accounting and disclosure policies, climate-change and Louisiana coastal-erosion lawsuits, management’s view that the claims are meritless and unlikely to materially harm ExxonMobil, and guarantees and long-term commitments. Note 17 presents pension and other postretirement benefit obligations, assumptions, costs, assets, funding status, balance-sheet and comprehensive-income effects, investment strategy and fair-value classifications for 2023–2024, underfunded plans, and expected 2025 contributions and future benefit payments.

title: Note 18. Disclosures about Segments and Related Information

nodes.title: Note 18. Disclosures about Segments and Related Information (intro)
nodes.summary: Note 18 describes ExxonMobil’s four reportable segments, their businesses, the Management Committee’s CODM role, resource and capital allocation, and use of attributable net income to assess performance. It presents 2022–2024 segment revenue, costs, income, assets, capital additions and equity investments, with reconciliations to consolidated totals and explanatory footnotes. It also reports customer-contract versus other revenue under ASC 606, geographic sales and significant non-U.S. revenue sources, and U.S./non-U.S. long-lived assets and major foreign locations.

nodes.title: Revenue from Contracts with Customers
nodes.summary: The notes explain that sales and other operating revenue includes both ASC 606 customer-contract revenue and revenue outside ASC 606, primarily from physically settled commodity derivative contracts. Contract terms, credit quality, and customer types are generally similar across both groups. A table presents these revenue categories and total sales for 2024, 2023, and 2022, in millions of dollars; no amounts are shown in the excerpt.

nodes.title: Geographic
nodes.summary: Geographic disclosures report 2022–2024 sales and operating revenue by U.S. and non-U.S. operations, identifying major non-U.S. revenue countries, and long-lived assets by region and key non-U.S. countries, with attribution caveats. Note 19 presents income taxes and other taxes and duties by location and year, deferred-tax effects of law changes, and the EU’s 2022 energy-sector windfall tax and resulting charges. It also reconciles tax expense to the 21% theoretical U.S. rate, showing pretax income, reconciliation factors, effective tax rates, and equity-company taxes.

nodes.title: Total
nodes.summary: The notes reconcile income tax expense to the 21% U.S. theoretical rate for 2022–2024, showing effective rates and the impact of equity-method income, foreign and state taxes, and other items, including additional European energy-sector taxes in 2022–2023. They detail deferred tax assets, liabilities, valuation allowances, balance-sheet classification, and indefinitely reinvested foreign earnings. They also explain uncertain tax-position recognition and annual movements, potential effects and resolution outlook, examination years by jurisdiction, and income-tax-related interest and penalties.

summary: Note 18 describes ExxonMobil’s four reportable segments, the Management Committee’s role as CODM, how it allocates resources and assesses performance, and segment results, assets, capital additions, and equity investments for 2022–2024, reconciled to consolidated totals. It also covers ASC 606 and other revenue, geographic sales and long-lived assets, and significant locations. Related tax disclosures address taxes by location, the EU windfall tax, reconciliations to the 21% U.S. rate, deferred taxes and foreign earnings, uncertain tax positions, examinations, and tax-related interest and penalties.

title: Note 20. Divestment Activities
summary: The Corporation’s divestments generated approximately $5.0 billion in proceeds and $1.0 billion in after-tax earnings in 2024; $4.1 billion and $0.6 billion in 2023; and $5.2 billion and $0.4 billion in 2022. Sales included named oil and gas, refining, and LNG assets in California, Nigeria, Argentina, France, Italy, Thailand, and the United States, plus a joint venture and assets in Romania and Canada, alongside other smaller divestments.

title: Note 21. Mergers and Acquisitions
summary: On May 3, 2024, ExxonMobil acquired Pioneer Natural Resources for 545 million ExxonMobil shares valued at $63 billion and assumed $5 billion of debt. The business combination was provisionally measured under ASC 805 at fair value: $88 billion in identifiable assets, $26 billion in liabilities, $62 billion in net identifiable assets, $1 billion in goodwill allocated to Upstream, and $63 billion in net assets. Notes describe valuation methods and inputs for receivables/payables, oil and gas properties, debt, deferred taxes, and the provisional one-year measurement period. Assumed debt included convertible and senior notes with listed par and acquisition-date fair values; all assumed convertible notes were redeemed in June 2024 at an amount consistent with acquisition-date fair value.

title: Actual and Pro Forma Impact of Merger

nodes.title: Actual and Pro Forma Impact of Merger (intro)
nodes.summary: Pioneer contributed $17.008 billion in revenue and $1.710 billion in net income attributable to ExxonMobil from its May 3, 2024 acquisition through year-end. Unaudited pro forma results, assuming the merger occurred January 1, 2023, show 2024 revenue of $347.406 billion and net income of $34.476 billion, versus $358.014 billion and $39.211 billion in 2023. Adjustments reflect merger-related, factually supportable effects, including accounting-policy alignment, acquired-asset depreciation, capital structure, transaction costs, and taxes. Results are not necessarily indicative of actual outcomes; acquisition transaction costs were immaterial.

nodes.title: Denbury Inc.
nodes.summary: On November 2, 2023, the Corporation acquired Denbury, a carbon capture, utilization, and storage developer and enhanced oil recovery producer with Gulf Coast and Rocky Mountain oil and gas operations. Consideration totaled $5.1 billion: 46 million ExxonMobil shares valued at $4.8 billion and $0.3 billion in cash for credit facility repayment and fractional shares. Accounted for as an ASC 805 business combination, the acquisition-date fair values were $7.0 billion in assets ($0.4 billion current, $6.4 billion property, plant and equipment, and $0.2 billion other) and $1.9 billion in liabilities ($0.3 billion current and $1.6 billion long-term), yielding $5.1 billion in net assets. Property valuations used assumptions for tariffs, pipeline throughput, commodity prices, production, operating expenses, and risk-adjusted discount rates. Goodwill was immaterial, as were Denbury’s 2023 revenues and earnings for pro forma disclosure.

nodes.title: SUPPLEMENTAL INFORMATION ON OIL AND GAS EXPLORATION AND PRODUCTION ACTIVITIES (unaudited)
nodes.summary: Unaudited supplemental oil and gas exploration and production results for 2024, 2023, and 2022 are presented in millions of dollars by region, separately for consolidated subsidiaries and equity companies. Tables report third-party sales, transfers, revenue, production costs, exploration expenses, depreciation and depletion, other taxes, related income tax, and producing-activity results and totals. Results exclude specified other Upstream activities and adjustments, which totaled $1,395 million in 2024, $(519) million in 2023, and $4,802 million in 2022; oil sands mining is included under SEC and FASB rules.

summary: Reports Pioneer’s actual contribution after its May 2024 acquisition and unaudited 2023–2024 pro forma results, explaining key adjustments and cautioning that pro forma figures are not predictive. Describes Denbury’s acquisition, consideration, purchase-price allocation, valuation assumptions, and immaterial goodwill and pro forma earnings. Also presents unaudited 2022–2024 regional oil and gas exploration and production results for subsidiaries and equity companies, with revenue, costs, taxes, and producing-activity results, noting excluded activities and the treatment of oil sands mining.

title: Oil and Gas Exploration and Production Costs
summary: The text explains that oil and gas net capitalized costs for consolidated subsidiaries are $9.619 billion lower in 2024 and $10.769 billion lower in 2023 than Upstream property, plant and equipment investments because certain transportation, research and LNG assets are excluded; oil sands and oil shale mining assets are included under FASB rules. It presents 2024 and 2023 capitalized-cost tables for consolidated subsidiaries and equity companies by geographic region, covering proved and unproved acreage, producing assets, construction, total costs, accumulated depreciation and depletion, and net capitalized costs.

title: Oil and Gas Exploration and Production Costs (continued)

nodes.title: Costs Incurred in Property Acquisitions, Exploration and Development Activities
nodes.summary: The text explains that oil and gas costs incurred include capitalized and expensed costs plus new or revised asset retirement obligations. Consolidated costs rose to $105.094 billion in 2024, mainly due to the Pioneer acquisition and higher development costs; 2023 costs rose to $20.952 billion, driven by development costs and Denbury. Equity-company costs fell to $1.134 billion in 2024 due to lower development costs. A 2022–2024 regional table details consolidated-subsidiary and equity-company costs for property acquisitions (proved and unproved), exploration, and development.

nodes.title: Oil and Gas Reserves
nodes.summary: Defines SEC-based proved reserves, including economic, operational, and contract conditions; explains pricing assumptions, revision causes, ownership and exclusions, treatment of equity and production-sharing reserves, and developed versus undeveloped reserves. Notes use of reserve volumes in depreciation and discounted-cash-flow calculations, explains gas-production reporting differences, and states that production-sharing contracts represented 11% of 2024 reserves. Summarizes 2022–2024 reserve changes from production, asset sales, acquisitions, discoveries, extensions, purchases, and revisions, including key regions and Russia expropriation.

nodes.title: Crude Oil, Natural Gas Liquids, Bitumen and Synthetic Oil Proved Reserves
nodes.summary: Tables report proved reserves of crude oil, natural gas liquids, bitumen, and synthetic oil in millions of barrels, by region and ownership type. They detail 2022–2024 annual movements—opening balances, revisions, recovery improvements, purchases, sales, discoveries/extensions, production, noncontrolling interests, and equity-company interests—and year-end totals. Separate year-end tables classify developed and undeveloped reserves for 2022, 2023, and 2024. A note identifies 118 million Russian barrels expropriated and refers readers to the 2024 Form 10-K for further natural-gas-liquids information.

nodes.title: Natural Gas and Oil-Equivalent Proved Reserves
nodes.summary: Tables report proved developed and undeveloped natural-gas reserves and oil-equivalent reserves for 2022–2024, by geographic region and for consolidated subsidiaries, noncontrolling interests, and equity companies. They show annual opening balances and reserve changes from revisions, improved recovery, purchases, sales, extensions/discoveries, and production, plus year-end totals. Separate tables break out developed versus undeveloped reserves for each year. Natural gas is converted at six billion cubic feet per million oil-equivalent barrels; a note identifies Russian reserves expropriated in 2022.

summary: Covers oil and gas acquisition, exploration and development costs, including capitalized and expensed amounts, asset-retirement obligations, regional cost categories, and major annual changes. Defines proved reserves and explains estimation assumptions, ownership, reserve classifications, production reporting, and use in depreciation and cash-flow calculations. Presents 2022–2024 regional reserve movements and year-end developed and undeveloped totals for crude oil, natural gas liquids, bitumen, synthetic oil, natural gas, and oil-equivalent reserves, including changes from production, revisions, recovery improvements, purchases, sales, discoveries, and extensions; notes Russian expropriations and the gas-to-oil-equivalent conversion.

title: Standardized Measure of Discounted Future Cash Flows
key_items: Standardized Measure of Discounted Future Cash Flows
summary: The standardized measure of discounted future net cash flows applies first-day-of-the-month average prices, year-end costs, legislated tax rates, and a 10% discount rate to proved reserves, including future dismantlement, abandonment, and rehabilitation costs. The Corporation cautions that prescribed assumptions—especially point-in-time prices—can cause significant year-to-year variability, so the measure is not a reliable estimate of expected cash flows from oil and gas development and production or of proved reserve value. The section is presented in millions of dollars.

title: As of December 31, 2022 Consolidated Subsidiaries
summary: Presents ExxonMobil’s standardized measure of discounted future oil and gas cash flows, in millions of dollars, by region for 2022, 2023, and 2024. For consolidated subsidiaries and equity companies, it lists projected sales inflows, production and development costs, income taxes, future net cash flows, the 10% discount effect, and discounted net cash flows, plus combined totals. Notes that Canada/Other Americas figures include discounted cash flows attributable to noncontrolling interests of $6.596 billion in 2022, $3.055 billion in 2023, and $4.466 billion in 2024.

title: Changes in Discounted Oil and Gas Reserve Cash Flows
key_items: Change in Standardized Measure of Discounted Future Net Cash Flows Relating to Proved Oil and Gas Reserves
summary: Presents 2022–2024 annual changes in the standardized measure of discounted future net cash flows from proved oil and gas reserves, in millions of dollars, for consolidated subsidiaries, equity method investees, and their combined totals. Each year reports opening and closing values and changes from reserve additions, production and transfers, development spending, prices and costs, reserve revisions, discount accretion, and income taxes.

title: INDEX TO EXHIBITS
summary: The exhibit index lists ExxonMobil’s charter, bylaws, capital-stock description, incentive and compensation plans, executive benefits, director grants and fees, and an aircraft time-share agreement, with incorporation-by-reference details and an asterisk marking compensatory arrangements. It also identifies the ethics and insider-trading policies, subsidiaries, auditor consent, executive and accounting-officer certifications, compensation-recovery policy, and Inline XBRL files. The registrant offers to provide long-term debt instruments to the SEC on request. The report is signed by Chairman Darren W. Woods on February 19, 2025.

title: POWER OF ATTORNEY
summary: The document includes a power of attorney authorizing three attorneys-in-fact to sign and file amendments to Exxon Mobil’s 2024 Form 10-K, followed by signatures dated February 19, 2025, for executive, financial, accounting officers and directors. It sets out 2024 stock-settled restricted stock unit terms: acceptance and credit, transfer restrictions, vesting dates, forfeiture conditions, tax withholding, dividend equivalents, adjustments, settlement, legal limits, privacy, employment disclaimers, governing law and entire agreement. It also summarizes a non-employee director’s 2,500-share restricted stock award, including ownership rights, transfer restrictions, release events, beneficiary designation and contacts.

title: CODE OF ETHICS AND BUSINESS CONDUCT

nodes.title: Ethics and Conflicts of Interest Policies
nodes.summary: Exxon Mobil requires compliance with applicable laws and the highest standards of integrity, fairness, and honesty, regardless of local customs or business pressures. Employees must accurately maintain books and records, cooperate candidly with auditors and management, follow policies and controls, and report material information to support full, fair, accurate, timely, and understandable public disclosures. Directors, officers, and employees must avoid actual or apparent conflicts, including misusing corporate opportunities or assets, trading on material nonpublic information, and competing with the Corporation.

nodes.title: Corporate Assets and Directorship Policies
nodes.summary: The assets policy requires directors, officers, and employees to protect and efficiently use corporate assets, including tangible assets and confidential or personal information, and forbids unauthorized use or disclosure of such information during or after service. The directorships policy restricts officers’ and employees’ service on nonaffiliated for-profit boards when it conflicts with or interferes with their duties; nonprofit roles are allowed unless they create such issues or obligate corporate support. Service on affiliated-company boards may be a work assignment. Public-company directorships held by corporate directors require Board approval; other nonaffiliated for-profit directorships require management approval as directed by the Chairman.

nodes.title: Procedures and Open Door Communication
nodes.summary: Exxon Mobil encourages employees to raise questions, concerns, and suggestions and promptly report suspected legal, policy, or internal-control violations, which management investigates; Internal Audit leads internal-control investigations, with objective judgment expected. Employees should start with supervisors, escalate as needed, or use relevant departments. Allegations involving directors or executives and accounting or auditing concerns go to the General Auditor, with board review procedures; anonymous complaints may be submitted by phone or mail, and accounting-related complaints go to the Audit Committee. Confidentiality is handled with discretion but cannot be guaranteed. Retaliation is prohibited unless reports are made with willful disregard for truth; dishonest or noncompliant conduct may lead to discipline. Foundation policies cannot be waived; employees should seek guidance, and approved situations are deemed nonviolations rather than exceptions.

nodes.title: EXHIBIT 19
nodes.summary: EXHIBIT 19

summary: The code requires compliance with law and high standards of integrity, accurate records and disclosures, cooperation with audits, and avoidance of conflicts, misuse of corporate opportunities, insider trading, or competition with the Corporation. It covers protecting corporate assets and confidential information, restrictions and approvals for outside directorships, and procedures for raising concerns and reporting violations, including investigations, escalation routes, anonymous complaints, confidentiality limits, anti-retaliation protections, discipline, and nonwaivable policies. It also identifies Exhibit 19.

title: EXXON MOBIL CORPORATION
key_items: Restrictions for Employees in Certain Positions; Violations of this Policy
Restrictions for Employees in Certain Positions
summary: ExxonMobil’s insider-trading policy requires directors, officers, employees, and relevant family members to avoid trading securities—including other companies’ securities—using material non-public information, sharing or tipping such information, or recommending trades; EMPT employees and their families may not use Company-stock derivatives. It defines material, non-public information and securities, gives examples, and explains position-based trading restrictions, plan-election limits, legal and disciplinary penalties, and Law Department guidance. For covered officers, directors, and related persons, it sets quarterly and special blackout periods; restricts specified trades, hedging, short sales, short-swing trades, and pledging; describes permitted transactions and pre-clearance; and governs approved Rule 10b5-1 plans and related public disclosures.

title: Subsidiaries of the Registrant (1), (2) and (3) – at December 31, 2024
summary: Exhibit 21 lists selected Registrant subsidiaries as of December 31, 2024, with each entity’s direct or indirect voting-security ownership percentage and state or country of organization. Notes explain the treatment of approximately 50%-owned entities, nominee and director qualifying shares, omitted immaterial subsidiaries, shared ownership, and equity-method accounting for unconsolidated investments. Exhibit 23 follows.

title: CONSENT OF INDEPENDENT REGISTERED PUBLIC ACCOUNTING FIRM
summary: PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP consents to incorporating by reference its February 19, 2025 report on Exxon Mobil Corporation’s financial statements and internal control over financial reporting into the specified Form S-3 and S-8 registration statements. The consent is signed in Houston, Texas, on February 19, 2025.

title: Certification by Darren W. Woods Pursuant to Securities Exchange Act Rule 13a-14(a)
summary: Exxon Mobil CEO Darren W. Woods certifies under Exchange Act Rule 13a-14(a) that he reviewed the 2024 Form 10-K; it contains no material misstatements or omissions, and its financial information fairly presents the company’s condition, operations, and cash flows. He and other certifying officers affirm responsibility for designing, evaluating, and reporting on disclosure controls and financial reporting controls, including material quarterly changes, and for informing auditors and the audit committee of significant control deficiencies, material weaknesses, and relevant fraud. Signed February 19, 2025.

title: Certification by Kathryn A. Mikells Pursuant to Securities Exchange Act Rule 13a-14(a)
summary: Exhibit 31.2 is Kathryn A. Mikells’s February 19, 2025 certification under Exchange Act Rule 13a-14(a) regarding Exxon Mobil’s Form 10-K. She certifies that she reviewed the report, it contains no materially misleading statements or omissions, and its financial information fairly presents the company’s condition and results. She describes officers’ responsibility for designing and evaluating disclosure controls and financial reporting controls, reporting material control changes, and disclosing significant deficiencies, material weaknesses, and relevant fraud to auditors and the audit committee. Mikells signs as Senior Vice President and CFO.

summary: Exhibits 31.3 and 32.1–32.3 contain certifications dated February 19, 2025, concerning Exxon Mobil’s 2024 Form 10-K. Principal Accounting Officer Len M. Fox certifies he reviewed the report, its material accuracy and fair financial presentation, and describes officers’ responsibilities for disclosure controls and financial reporting controls, including evaluation, reporting changes, and disclosure of deficiencies, weaknesses, and relevant fraud. CEO Darren W. Woods, CFO Kathryn A.
